builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
summary: SplitBench replaces monolithic benchmark harnesses, in which the agent's executed code shares privileges with the grading logic, with a privilege-separated design where a trusted grader holding expected answers is isolated from the test environment the agent can compromise. The cost is engineering effort to port existing benchmarks (22 of 202 tasks did not convert) plus the added complexity of maintaining a separate trusted grading component, with no claim of reduced compute or latency. After adoption, residual failures come mainly from weaknesses in the original tasks' tests (the 25% of adversarial attempts that succeeded) and from imperfect conversion fidelity (about 1.3% disagreement with native graders).
rationale: Benchmark integrity directly affects model and vendor selection, and privilege separation is a low-infrastructure change to evaluation harnesses rather than a model capability, so any team running coding-agent benchmarks should adopt the separation principle and test the framework on their specific suites.

claims.statement: SplitBench replaces monolithic benchmark harnesses, in which the agent's executed code shares privileges with the grading logic, with a privilege-separated design where a trusted grader holding expected answers is isolated from the test environment the agent can compromise. The cost is engineering effort to port existing benchmarks (22 of 202 tasks did not convert) plus the added complexity of maintaining a separate trusted grading component, with no claim of reduced compute or latency. After adoption, residual failures come mainly from weaknesses in the original tasks' tests (the 25% of adversarial attempts that succeeded) and from imperfect conversion fidelity (about 1.3% disagreement with native graders).

SplitBench agrees with native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts, 180 of 202 tasks convert, and it blocked 75% of worst-case adversarial attempts; these are correctness/coverage figures, not a performance gain over a baseline technique.
